chief_complaint: brief loss of consciousness following skateboard fall, now presenting with rapid neurological decline and fixed dilated pupil
hpi_details: 21M skateboarder fell and struck right temporal region on concrete curb without helmet. Experienced brief loss of consciousness (~2 minutes) followed by a 4-hour lucid interval where he walked home and conversed normally. Over the past hour, developed severe progressive headache, vomiting, lethargy, and left-sided hemiparesis. Brought to ED by roommates unresponsive.
ideas: roommates alarmed because he woke up screaming of headache then collapsed into coma
concerns: roommates worried he suffered catastrophic brain bleeding
expectations: want immediate emergency brain surgery to save his life

investigation_events.title: Emergency head CT
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency CT result is now available. Airway protection, hyperosmolar therapy, and operative transfer should not be delayed.

results.value: Right temporal biconvex hyperdense extra-axial hematoma, 2.8 cm thick, with 12 mm leftward midline shift and uncal herniation; temporal bone fracture crosses the middle meningeal artery groove

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Epidural Hematoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Epidural Hematoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes STAT neurosurgical emergency: immediate transfer to operating room for right temporal craniotomy, evacuation of epidural hematoma, and hemostasis of middle meningeal artery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: brief loss of consciousness following skateboard fall, now presenting with rapid neurological decline and fixed dilated pupil

Key HPI features: 21M skateboarder fell and struck right temporal region on concrete curb without helmet. Experienced brief loss of consciousness (~2 minutes) followed by a 4-hour lucid interval where he walked home and conversed normally. Over the past hour, developed severe progressive headache, vomiting, lethargy, and left-sided hemiparesis. Brought to ED by roommates unresponsive.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 48, BP 178/95 (Cushing reflex bradycardia and hypertension), Temp 36.8C. GCS 6 (E1 V1 M4 - withdrawing to pain on right, decerebrate posturing on left). Right pupil 7 mm fixed and non-reactive to light; left pupil 3 mm reactive. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense extra-axial collection over the right temporal lobe measuring 2.8 cm in depth with 12 mm leftward midline shift and uncal transtentorial herniation. Underlying skull fracture of squamous temporal bone across middle meningeal artery groove.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Epidural Hematoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute subdural hematoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: A fixed dilated pupil signals uncal herniation, a neurosurgical emergency.
management_principles: STAT neurosurgical emergency: immediate transfer to operating room for right temporal craniotomy, evacuation of epidural hematoma, and hemostasis of middle meningeal artery
Intubate for airway protection and hyperventilate mildly (PaCO2 30-35 mmHg) during transit
Administer IV Mannitol 1g/kg or hypertonic saline bolus to acutely reduce ICP
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 21M presenting with classic history of acute epidural hematoma: head trauma, brief syncope, lucid interval, and rapid secondary neurological deterioration.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 48, BP 178/95 (Cushing reflex bradycardia and hypertension), Temp 36.8C. GCS 6 (E1 V1 M4 - withdrawing to pain on right, decerebrate posturing on left). Right pupil 7 mm fixed and non-reactive to light; left pupil 3 mm reactive. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense extra-axial collection over the right temporal lobe measuring 2.8 cm in depth with 12 mm leftward midline shift and uncal transtentorial herniation. Underlying skull fracture of squamous temporal bone across middle meningeal artery groove.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Right Temporal Epidural Hematoma secondary to middle meningeal artery disruption with uncal herniation and elevated intracranial pressure.
reference_soap.plan: STAT neurosurgical emergency: immediate transfer to operating room for right temporal craniotomy, evacuation of epidural hematoma, and hemostasis of middle meningeal artery. Intubate for airway protection and hyperventilate mildly (PaCO2 30-35 mmHg) during transit. Administer IV Mannitol 1g/kg or hypertonic saline bolus to acutely reduce ICP. Elevate head of bed 30 degrees.

learning_objectives: Recognize classic pathognomonic progression of acute epidural hematoma (trauma, syncope, lucid interval, rapid herniation)
Correlate ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III compression) and contralateral hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle compression) with uncal herniation
Identify biconvex hyperdense extra-axial hematoma morphology on non-contrast head CT
Outline immediate acute ICP management protocols prior to emergency craniotomy

teaching.one_liner: A tear in the middle meningeal artery from head trauma causes bleeding between the skull and the dura, classically producing a lucid interval: the patient seems fine for hours before rapidly deteriorating as the clot expands.
red_flags: A fixed dilated pupil signals uncal herniation, a neurosurgical emergency

must_ask.say: Did he lose consciousness right after the fall, and for how long?
Did he seem completely normal for a while after the fall, before getting worse?
How has his headache, vomiting, and alertness changed in the past hour?
Is one side of his body weaker than the other?

history.answer: He fell off his skateboard earlier today and hit his head, and now he is completely unresponsive and won't wake up.
He has always been completely sharp and healthy, and he goes to college full-time with no memory or thinking problems.
He fell and hit his head about five hours ago, seemed fine for a while, but then crashed suddenly about an hour ago.
Right after getting knocked out for a couple of minutes, he woke up, walked home with us, and talked completely normally for four hours.
About an hour ago he became very sleepy and confused, and now he doesn't respond at all when we call his name or shake him.
He was skateboarding on the street, lost his balance, and hit the right side of his head hard against a concrete curb.
No, he was not wearing a helmet when he fell.
Yes, he was knocked out cold for about two minutes right after hitting the curb before waking back up.
No, he does not take aspirin, blood thinners, or any medications like that.
Right before passing out, he couldn't move his left arm and leg properly and his speech was slurring.
An hour ago he woke up screaming from a terrible headache, and then he threw up violently twice.
No, he did not have any shaking fits, he did not bite his tongue, and he did not wet himself.
No, he hasn't had any fever, chills, cough, or trouble when peeing.
He didn't complain of a stiff neck, and there are no strange spots or rashes on his body.
He does not have diabetes, he doesn't take insulin, and he ate lunch normally earlier today.
He was eating and drinking fine all afternoon until he started vomiting an hour ago.
He has not started or changed any medications, and he doesn't take sleeping pills or pain medicine.
He hasn't had any alcohol today, and there were no empty pill bottles or recreational drugs around.
He couldn't tell us if he had double vision, but he stumbled and lost his balance right before collapsing.
No, our apartment heater is working fine, there is no gas smell, and none of the rest of us feel sick.
No, he has never had liver or kidney disease, no yellow eyes, and no belly swelling.
No, he has no history of depression or psychiatric conditions, and this has never happened before.
We were terrified when he woke up screaming in pain and passed out; we're worried he has severe bleeding in his brain.
We think he needs an immediate emergency brain operation right now to save his life.
He is twenty-one and has always been completely healthy with no chronic medical conditions.
He has never had any surgeries and has never stayed in a hospital.
He does not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or vitamins.
He does not have any known allergies to medicines.
No, he has never smoked cigarettes and does not vape.
He only drinks an occasional beer socially once or twice a month, and he hasn't had any drinks in the past week.
He is an undergraduate college student and lives in an apartment with two roommates.
Both of his parents are healthy, and there is no family history of aneurysms, bleeding disorders, or early brain disease.

exam.finding: Young adult male lying unresponsive on the examination gurney with abnormal posturing and no spontaneous speech.
Blood pressure is 178/95 mmHg, heart rate is 48 beats/min, respiratory rate is 12 breaths/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and fingerstick blood glucose is 112 mg/dL.
Contusion, hematoma, and superficial abrasion noted over the right squamous temporal scalp; no open lacerations or skull step-offs palpated.
Right pupil is 7 mm, fixed, and non-reactive to direct and consensual light; left pupil is 3 mm and briskly reactive to light.
Both tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray without hemotympanum, discharge, or retroauricular ecchymosis.
Oral cavity is clear with no tongue lacerations, bite marks, or active bleeding; airway is currently unprotected.
Sclerae are non-icteric and conjunctivae are pink without pallor or petechiae.
Comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6 (eye opening 1, verbal response 1, motor response 4 - purposeful withdrawal to pain on the right).
Right-sided extremities withdraw purposefully to noxious stimuli (M4); left-sided extremities show decerebrate extensor posturing with adduction and internal rotation.
Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes on the left side with an extensor plantar response (positive Babinski sign); right-sided reflexes are 2+ with a flexor plantar response.
Neck is supple without resistance to passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
